items.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019
items.q: And so Dizzy, he was a master at it. So was Charlie Parker.

ctx.x: Do you think that he thought there was no such things as wrong notes in improvising. I’m not sure I asked that very well, but the idea that there are wrong notes when you improvise, I wonder if —

I’ll say it this way. There are no wrong notes but there are wrong lines. And so relief is a half step away. And so Dizzy and Miles and those cats, they were masters of non- harmonic tones with the proper resolutions. Because the whole chromatic scale can be related to one triad if you resolve everything properly. And so if you land wrong, man, you could make it an appoggiatura, a step up into the chord. And so Dizzy, he was a master at it. So was Charlie Parker. So there are only wrong notes if you play the…

Well said. I wanted to read something about you from the three volume Grove Dictionary of Jazz, which you’re in. And this person, whoever wrote this, he says, “Mike’s style as a pianist is based on those of Oscar Peterson and Bud Powell, to which he has added a personal and contemplative approach.”
